blogs.title: When Angioedema Isn't: A Framework for Subacute Neck Swelling That Defies Classic Pathways
blogs.description: This post explores the diagnostic approach to subacute neck swelling that doesn't fit histamine-mediated or bradykinin-mediated angioedema patterns. Using the case as a springboard, it reviews the key clinical features that should raise suspicion for non-angioedema causes—including absence of ACE inhibitors or DPP-4 inhibitors, no family/personal history of angioedema, normal complement and C1 esterase levels, and associated systemic findings such as muscle weakness or skin changes. The post outlines a practical diagnostic algorithm for emergency physicians and immunologists when 'idiopathic angioedema' doesn't add up, emphasizing the importance of broadening the differential to include inflammatory myopathies, superior vena cava syndrome, and orofacial granulomatosis.

blogs.title: The $7 Test That Reframed the Entire Differential: Why CK Belongs in the Workup of Unexplained Swelling
blogs.description: This post focuses on the pivotal role of a single creatine kinase level in redirecting the diagnostic trajectory of this case. It discusses when CK should be checked in patients presenting with unexplained soft tissue swelling, particularly when accompanied by subtle weakness, myalgia, or dysphagia. The post reviews the differential of a markedly elevated CK (>10,000 U/L) and how it distinguishes inflammatory myopathy from other causes of neck swelling. It also addresses common pitfalls: why muscle weakness can be subtle early in the disease course, why proximal weakness may be missed on casual exam, and how elevated transaminases in the setting of normal liver function can be a clue that the 'liver enzymes' are actually coming from muscle.

blogs.title: Anti-SAE1 Dermatomyositis: What This Rare Antibody Tells Us About Phenotype, Prognosis, and Where Myositis Classification Is Heading
blogs.description: This post dives into the expanding world of myositis-specific antibodies and how they are reshaping classification, prognosis, and management of inflammatory myopathies. It reviews the clinical phenotype of anti-SAE1 dermatomyositis—including its high rates of dysphagia (~46%), interstitial lung disease (~43%), and malignancy association (~18%)—and compares it to other key antibody subtypes (anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1γ, anti-Mi-2, anti-Jo-1). The post discusses how antibody profiling can guide malignancy screening intensity, ILD surveillance, and prognostic counseling, even when the classic cutaneous features of dermatomyositis (Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash) are absent.

blogs.title: Dysphagia in Dermatomyositis: More Than Just Proximal Weakness, and Why It Drives Both Morbidity and Malignancy Risk
blogs.description: This post examines dysphagia as an underappreciated but high-impact manifestation of dermatomyositis. Using the case's severe pharyngeal dysphagia requiring prolonged nasogastric feeding, it reviews the mechanisms of swallowing dysfunction in inflammatory myopathies— encompassing both striated muscle involvement of the pharynx and upper esophagus and potential cricopharyngeal dysfunction. The post covers practical assessment tools (video fluoroscopic swallow studies), aspiration risk stratification, and the clinical significance of dysphagia as both a driver of morbidity (aspiration pneumonitis, prolonged hospitalization, malnutrition) and a marker of malignancy risk per the IMACS cancer screening guidelines. It also addresses how dysphagia resolution can lag behind other markers of disease improvement.

blogs.title: Cancer Screening in Dermatomyositis: Navigating the IMACS Risk Stratification Framework in Practice
blogs.description: This post explores the complex topic of malignancy screening in dermatomyositis, using the IMACS (International Myositis Assessment and Clinical Studies Group) guideline framework applied in this case. It reviews the evidence linking dermatomyositis to malignancy, the specific risk factors that elevate malignancy probability (dysphagia, male sex, anti-SAE1 and anti-TIF1γ antibodies, older age at onset), and the practical approach to baseline and interval surveillance. The post discusses the role of CT imaging, PET-CT, tumor markers, and endoscopic evaluation, while addressing the tension between thorough screening and the risk of over-investigation, cost, and patient burden in a relatively young patient.

blogs.title: Multi-Agent Immunosuppression in Severe Dermatomyositis: Rationale, Evidence Gaps, and the Art of Drug Selection
blogs.description: This post analyzes the immunosuppressive strategy used in this case—IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone taper, IVIG, rituximab, and mycophenolate mofetil—and the rationale behind each choice. It reviews the limited evidence base guiding treatment of severe, antibody-specific dermatomyositis and discusses why methotrexate was deliberately avoided (pulmonary concerns), why azathioprine and tacrolimus were not selected, and the emerging role of rituximab and IVIG in refractory or rapidly progressive disease. The post also covers the practical challenges of opportunistic infection prophylaxis (including the patient's hemolytic anemia on TMP-SMX requiring switch to nebulized pentamidine) and the sequencing of immunosuppressive agents in a patient with dysphagia, aspiration risk, and potential ILD.
